text: David Edward Crombie PC OC OOnt (born April 24, 1936) is a former Canadian academic and politician who served as the 56th mayor of Toronto from 1972 to 1978. After his mayoral tenure, he was elected to Parliament as a member of the Progressive Conservative (PC) Party. He held several federal ministerial positions: minister of national health and welfare from 1979 to 1980, minister of Indian affairs and northern development from 1984 to 1986, and secretary of state for Canada from 1986 to 1988. Born in Swansea, a village west of Toronto, to Vera Edith (Beamish) and Norman Davis Crombie, he was a lecturer in politics and urban affairs at Ryerson in the 1960s when he became involved in Toronto's urban reform movement. At the time, the city council supported extensive development, including demolition of older buildings for apartment blocks, office towers, and highways such as the Spadina Expressway. Crombie, alongside John Sewell and other reformers, led a grassroots effort to limit development and prioritize social services and community interests. Elected to Toronto city council in 1970, he became mayor in 1972, marking the first mayor to represent the reform movement and introducing socially responsible urban development inspired by Jane Jacobs. He sought to curb the development industry by initially imposing a 45-foot (13.7 m) height limit on new constructions, which was overturned by the Ontario Municipal Board; he later introduced a city-wide official plan with varying height restrictions, which was upheld. While Premier Bill Davis had halted the Spadina Expressway in 1971, he continued to support the Allen Expressway, which Crombie failed to stop, though he successfully halted the Scarborough Expressway, leading to its cancellation. Crombie opposed demolishing poorer neighborhoods for housing projects and ended redevelopment plans for Trefann Court, Kensington Market, and Cabbagetown. Instead, he oversaw the creation of the St. Lawrence neighborhood, a mid-rise, mixed-use, mixed-income area aligned with Jane Jacobs’s urban planning vision. He was re-elected in 1974 and 1976 with large majorities and was frequently described in the media as the city's "tiny, perfect mayor" due to his height of 5 feet 5 inches (1.65 m). He left City Hall in 1978 to enter federal politics, winning a by-election in the Rosedale electoral district against Liberal candidate John Evans, who was weakened by the Liberals' unpopularity and a competitive nomination challenge by Anne Cools. Crombie defeated Cools in the 1979 and 1980 general elections and future foreign minister Bill Graham in 1984. He served as Minister of Health and Welfare in Prime Minister Joe Clark’s short-lived minority government from 1979 to 1980. In September 1979, as minister, he stated the federal government’s commitment to collaborating with Indigenous representatives in reviewing Indian health issues, allowing for policy changes based on their input. The previous year, Indigenous groups such as the Union of B.C. Chiefs, the Native Brotherhood, and the United Native Nations had lobbied for greater control over health services and the repeal of restrictive guidelines related to mercury and fluoride pollution. Crombie appointed Gary Goldthorpe as commissioner of the federal inquiry (the Goldthorpe Inquiry) into alleged medical care abuses in Alert Bay, British Columbia. In 1979, Justice Thomas Berger, leading the royal commission on Indigenous and Inuit healthcare, recommended greater consultation with Indigenous peoples and an annual allocation of $950,000 to the National Indian Brotherhood for developing health consultation structures; Crombie’s successor, Monique Begin, adopted these recommendations, initiating a shift in health delivery. At the 1983 Progressive Conservative leadership convention, Crombie was the only candidate to campaign as a "Red Tory," drawing support from moderates opposed to Joe Clark’s leadership. He finished fifth with 3.9% of delegate votes on the first ballot and would have been eliminated had not Michael Wilson, who was fourth with 4.8%, withdrawn. He was eliminated on the second ballot with only 2.3% of the votes and endorsed third-place candidate John Crosbie. After Brian Mulroney led the Conservatives to power in 1984, Crombie became minister of Indian affairs and northern development, then secretary of state for Canada and minister of multiculturalism. Frustrated in Ottawa as a Red Tory in a more conservative government, he chose not to run in the 1988 election and returned to urban affairs as head of the royal commission on the future of Toronto’s waterfront from 1988 to 1992. He authored influential reports, including Watershed and Regeneration, which proposed integrated, sustainable planning approaches. The provincial government appointed him head of the Waterfront Regeneration Trust Agency (1992–1999) to implement the 83 recommendations from Regeneration, including the creation of a waterfront trail. Today, the Great Lakes Waterfront Trail extends from Quebec to Sault Ste. Marie along Canada’s Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River. In 1999, Crombie founded the Waterfront Regeneration Trust as a charity to continue the agency’s work and serves on its board. The charity manages a fund for the protection and restoration of the Rouge Valley, now part of the Rouge National Urban Park. He attempted to find an alternative to the Red Hill Creek Expressway, but the Hamilton city council rejected his compromise proposal as insufficient. In 1994, Crombie was appointed Ryerson’s first chancellor when the institution received university status and served until 1999. Throughout the 1990s, he provided advisory services to city and provincial governments on urban issues in the Toronto area. In 2007, he retired as CEO of the Canadian Urban Institute. In April 2008, the Toronto District School Board selected him to negotiate keeping unfunded school swimming pools open to the public. In 2014, he publicly opposed plans by the federally run Toronto Port Authority to extend runways at Billy Bishop Airport on the Toronto Islands to allow Porter Airlines to operate jet planes. On May 13, 2004, he was appointed an Officer of the Order of Canada; in 2012, he became a member of the Order of Ontario; in 2013, he was inducted into the Canadian Disability Hall of Fame. He serves on the Governors' Council of the Toronto Public Library Foundation, the Honorary Council for the Loran Scholars Foundation, and the boards of CivicAction and the Planet in Focus Foundation, and is a member of the Patron’s Council at Dying with Dignity Canada. He also serves on advisory boards for the Ryerson Image Centre and CARP Canada. Crombie remains active in public discourse, often joining former mayors on the left—Art Eggleton, Barbara Hall, David Miller, and John Sewell—in issuing open letters on key issues. A park named after him runs from Jarvis Street to Berkeley Street in a former industrial area converted to housing. He is the father of two daughters, Robin and Carrie, and actor Jonathan Crombie, who starred in three Anne of Green Gables TV series. Jonathan died in New York on April 15, 2015, from a brain hemorrhage at age 48; his organs were donated, he was cremated, and his ashes were returned to Canada.
